course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 4
unit.description: Follow the rise of party politics and a more participatory democracy, the market revolution, westward expansion and foreign policy, the Second Great Awakening and reform, and the growth of slavery from 1800 to 1848.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Southern business leaders in the early 1800s continued to rely mainly on
choices: the manufacture of textiles and iron goods for sale in Northern markets
the production and export of agricultural staples such as cotton
shipbuilding and trade with Asia carried in fleets owned by Southern merchants
the mining of coal and iron for the railroads that linked the Southern states
questions.explanation: Dependence on cotton and other staple crops shaped the South's economy and its distinct regional identity.
choiceExplanations: Southern manufacturing was limited.
Dependence on cotton and other staple crops shaped the South's economy and its distinct regional identity.
Northern merchants dominated shipping.
Mining was not the basis of the Southern economy.
questions.distinguisher: The textile manufacturing choice is close because Southern cotton supplied textile mills, but the mills were mainly in the North and Britain.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why many planters moved from the Southeast to Alabama and Mississippi?
choices: The federal government ordered planters to move west after the slave trade ended
Northern factories had offered to buy the land of the Southeastern planters
Native nations in the West had invited planters to settle on their lands
Overcultivation had worn out the soil, and the western lands were more fertile
questions.explanation: Tobacco and cotton exhausted the soil of the Southeast, so planters sought richer land.
choiceExplanations: No order required planters to move.
No such offers drove the move.
Native nations were removed from those lands.
Tobacco and cotton exhausted the soil of the Southeast, so planters sought richer land.
questions.distinguisher: The federal order choice is close because government policy opened western lands, but planters chose to move.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: What was an effect of the westward movement of slavery on enslaved people?
choices: About a million were moved to the Deep South, often splitting families
Many were freed by planters who moved west and no longer needed their labor
Most moved to Northern cities, where they found work in mills and factories
Their number fell after 1808 as the Atlantic slave trade ended
questions.explanation: The internal slave trade forced a very large migration, and traders sold people in markets in Richmond and New Orleans.
choiceExplanations: The internal slave trade forced a very large migration, and traders sold people in markets in Richmond and New Orleans.
Slavery expanded and few were freed.
Most remained in the South.
The enslaved population grew.
questions.distinguisher: The freed choice is close because some planters did free enslaved people, but this was rare.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes slaveholding among white Southerners?
choices: Most white families owned at least one enslaved person and depended on that labor
Only a few hundred white families in the entire South owned enslaved people
Most white families owned no enslaved people, but large planters held great power
Most large planters lived in Northern cities and hired overseers to run the farms
questions.explanation: Slaveholders were a minority of white Southerners, yet planters dominated Southern politics and defended slavery as a way of life.
choiceExplanations: About three-fourths of white families owned none.
Many thousands of families owned enslaved people.
Slaveholders were a minority of white Southerners, yet planters dominated Southern politics and defended slavery as a way of life.
Large planters usually lived in the South.
questions.distinguisher: The at-least-one choice is close because slaveholding was widespread in some areas, but most families owned none.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following helps to explain why Southern leaders began to defend slavery as a “positive good” after the 1830s?
choices: A Supreme Court decision that ordered the nation to protect slavery in every state
Growing abolitionism in the North and the profits that cotton and slavery brought
A decline in cotton prices that made slavery less profitable and forced new arguments
A decision by Congress to end slavery gradually in the Southern states
questions.explanation: As abolitionists attacked slavery, Southern leaders shifted from calling it a necessary evil to defending it.
choiceExplanations: The Court issued no such decision in the 1830s.
As abolitionists attacked slavery, Southern leaders shifted from calling it a necessary evil to defending it.
Cotton prices and profits were high for much of the period.
Congress did not act to end slavery.
questions.distinguisher: The Supreme Court choice is close because the Court later decided slavery cases, but it did not cause the shift in the 1830s.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a difference between the Southern and Northern economies by the 1840s?
choices: The South had more factories, banks, and cities than the North
The North depended mainly on exporting cotton, while the South relied on mills
The South attracted most immigrants, while the North had few new workers
The South invested in land and enslaved laborers, while the North invested in factories
questions.explanation: Southern wealth was tied up in land and slaves, while the North invested in industry and transportation.
choiceExplanations: The North had more of each.
The roles were reversed.
Most immigrants went north.
Southern wealth was tied up in land and slaves, while the North invested in industry and transportation.
questions.distinguisher: The more factories choice is close because the South did have some industry, but the North had far more.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: The growth of a distinctive Southern regional identity is best understood in the context of which of the following?
choices: An economy based on cotton and slavery that differed from the North's
A decline in the importance of agriculture in the South and a turn to commerce
A federal decision to divide the nation into separate regions with their own laws
A wave of immigration into the South that brought new customs from Europe
questions.explanation: Southerners shared an economy of staple crops and enslaved labor, which set them apart from the market economy of the North.
choiceExplanations: Southerners shared an economy of staple crops and enslaved labor, which set them apart from the market economy of the North.
Agriculture remained central to the South.
No such decision was made.
The South received few immigrants.
questions.distinguisher: The decline of agriculture choice is close because the North was changing, but the South remained agricultural.
questions.subskillText: Identify and describe a historical context for a specific historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which geographic factor most helped the growth of cotton farming in the Deep South?
choices: Cold winters that killed pests and gave farmers a long period for planting
A long growing season and fertile soil in the Mississippi Valley and the Gulf plains
Mountains that sheltered the cotton fields from storms and from the sun
Deserts that held water and made large fields easy to irrigate
questions.explanation: The warm, wet climate and rich soil of the Deep South suited cotton and made new land attractive.
choiceExplanations: Cotton needs a long, warm growing season.
The warm, wet climate and rich soil of the Deep South suited cotton and made new land attractive.
Cotton was grown on plains and river valleys.
The Deep South was not a desert.
questions.distinguisher: The cold winters choice is close because winter frost affects pests, but cotton requires a long warm season.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a reason that many white Southerners who owned no enslaved people supported slavery?
choices: Slaveholders paid them to vote for proslavery candidates in each election
The Constitution required every white family to own enslaved people
Many hoped to own enslaved people, and slavery gave them higher status
Slavery had made them wealthy and given them control of most of the land
questions.explanation: Many yeoman farmers hoped to rise in society and valued the racial status that slavery gave them.
choiceExplanations: No such system existed.
The Constitution had no such requirement.
Many yeoman farmers hoped to rise in society and valued the racial status that slavery gave them.
Most nonslaveholders were small farmers with modest wealth.
questions.distinguisher: The payment choice is close because some planters influenced politics, but no payment system explained support.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.
